newsitem.title: USA: Fidelity says no talks yet with British regulators.
newsitem.headline: Fidelity says no talks yet with British regulators.

text.p: British regulators said Friday they would take action against Fidelity Investments' retail brokerage arm in England for customer service problems but did not specify what steps would be taken.
Fidelity Brokerage Services of Britain, owned by Boston-based Fidelity, the biggest mutual fund company in the United States, said it had not had talks with the regulators.
"We have not had specific discussions with the SFA (Securities and Futures Authority)," Phil West, marketing manager for Fidelity Brokerage Services, said by telephone from London.

Fidelity Brokerage Services promised in November to restore satisfactory service by January after computer glitches caused accounting and other problems, and promised compensation to customers who had lost out as a result.
But the brokerage continues to have problems "in the administration of accounts," West conceded, adding that the firm has not taken on any new customers since the problem was discovered last year.
He said the problems had caused a loss of "less than 1 percent of our client base."
The SFA declined to specify the range of penalties Fidelity may face, but it does have the power to impose fines or withdraw licenses both from individual investors and brokerage firms.
The problems in Britain, which surfaced in November, are the latest to confront Fidelity, whose stock funds, notably Magellan, posted their worst performance last year since 1980.

West said the problems included not paying dividends on time and not providing timely statements to customers. The problems, which stemmed from a new software system installed last summer, did not extend to execution of orders, he said.

In announcing the start of disciplinary action, the British agency said that "good progress has been made, but further work is still required before SFA can be confident that Fidelity Brokerage Services is offering a level of customer service which is consistently satisfactory."
The authority said it would continue to monitor Fidelity's customer service and would oversee the resolution of outstanding customer complaints and enquiries.
It said it would take into account how fast Fidelity resolved outstanding problems "in determining the nature and extent of disciplinary proceedings and the scale of the penalty which is sought."

The agency also extended restrictions imposed on Fidelity to the end of April. The moves stop it from taking on new direct customers or introducing new services. It said it was satisfied the firm had the resources to ensure investors' funds and securities were "not in any jeopardy."
Separately, despite poor returns last year, Magellan manager Robert Stansky said he was not under pressure from Fidelity management to buy certain stocks or invest in specific market sectors.

Stansky, who took over the nation's largest stock fund last June, said at a meeting with Fidelity investors late on Thursday that Magellan was being run as former managers Peter Lynch, Morris Smith and others ran the fund, by buying companies whose earnings are consistently growing.

Stansky succeeded Jeffrey Vinik, who left Fidelity in May after making a big bet on bonds that proved disastrous for Magellan. The meeting was one of several Fidelity has held recently with investors.
